# Building, testing and measuring blaze

<!-- Generated by `bun tools/agents/rules.ts --write` from tools/agents/rules.ts, down to the end marker; edit the rules there. AGENTS.md carries each rule as one line. -->

## blaze-builds-blaze (rule 2)

Build, check and test blaze with blaze (`blaze build`, `blaze check`, `blaze test`), never `cargo`,
`rustc` or sccache, in any place: an agent's loop, a harness, a CI workflow, a benchmark, the
release build or a doc's instructions. Stage 0 is a blaze binary (the release
`.github/blaze-version` names, or a blaze built earlier), never cargo, until the wasm seed replaces
it (docs/future/bootstrap.md). Stage 0 is never overwritten: a build of the tree (stage 1) becomes
stage 0 only after it rebuilds the tree (stage 2) byte for byte and the tests pass, and moving
`.github/blaze-version` forward is that promotion. When stage 0 can't build the tree, that is a
named error: write the source around it for one release or pin an older release, never cargo. Every
build, check, test and verdict comes from blaze. When blaze fails on blaze (a compile error, a link
error, a panic, a hang, a wrong result, too slow, too much memory), that failure is the work: fix
blaze, never route around it through cargo. A crate blaze can't check or test yet is a ranked, owned
blocker, not a reason to keep using cargo for it.

See [docs/contributing.md](../../../docs/contributing.md).

## verify-on-real-projects (rule 7)

A verdict on blaze comes from real projects built by blaze: blaze itself, then large open-source
workspaces (ripgrep, nushell, bevy, wasmtime, tokio, ...), each built with `blaze build` and its own
tests run with `blaze test`. A project whose tests pass under blaze is correct for what they cover;
a failing test is a blaze bug to fix. Never build a project with rustc or cargo to diff against: no
reference build, no output comparison with rustc's, no harness that runs cargo for an oracle. A
test's expectation states what is right, not what rustc printed.

See [docs/harness.md](../../../docs/harness.md).

## own-nightly (rule 8)

blaze is its own toolchain: it builds every project with its pinned nightly (`harness/toolchain`,
bumped daily), ignoring rust-toolchain files, rustup, `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN` and `RUSTC`. Projects pin
the blaze version, not Rust's.

See [docs/toolchain.md](../../../docs/toolchain.md).

## measure-the-exact-tree (rule 22)

A measurement, bisect or checkpoint names the exact tree it ran on (a content digest of the sources
and the blaze binary's hash) and keeps that tree; never re-sync or rebuild between measuring and
committing. A result you can't tie to a tree is not evidence.

## work-in-ix-vms (rule 34)

Builds, tests, benchmarks and experiments run on the Mac or in an ix VM (`ix new`, `ix shell`, `ix
rm`), never on AWS. Where neither can do it, stop and say what is missing.

See [docs/contributing.md#working-in-parallel](../../../docs/contributing.md#working-in-parallel).

## fan-out-write-only (rule 35)

Fan out code, not builds. Subagents only read and write code, including the tests for it. They never
run a build, check, test, clippy, benchmark or any other expensive step, and never start a daemon or
a VM. The main agent waits until every subagent has finished writing, applies all their changes to
one tree, and then runs it once: `blaze check` and `blaze test` (the central loop), with keep-going.
It hands each failure back to a fresh subagent for the code that broke, with the exact tree, the
command and the error, and runs again. Checks that need a variant tree, such as reverting a fix to
show its test fails (test-the-cause), are also run by the main agent, as patches.

## worktree-per-lane (rule 36)

One uniquely named worktree per lane; its build directory is its own under blaze's root, never in
the checkout, so it needs no `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`; never `git stash`.

## clean-up-lane (rule 39)

When a lane is done, delete its build directory (`blaze clean`), worktree, ix VM and merged branch.

<!-- End of the generated rules. Hand-written notes follow. -->

## How a lane runs

From [docs/contributing.md#working-in-parallel](../../../docs/contributing.md#working-in-parallel):

- Worktree: `git worktree add -b <branch> ../blaze-<lane>-<date> origin/main`. Commit work in
  progress to the lane's branch instead of stashing.
- VM: `ix new --name <lane> --no-shell` (`--cpus`, `--memory`, `--memory-commit` for a build,
  `--arch x86_64|arm64`, `--ttl 8h`); run with `ix shell <lane> -- <command>`; send a checkout with
  `git bundle create - <branch> | ix shell <lane> -- bash -c 'cat > src.bundle && git clone -b <branch> src.bundle src'`.
  The VM has no GitHub or AWS credentials. A benchmark gets its own VM pinned to a host CPU class
  (`--cpu epyc-5`, `xeon-6` or `graviton-5`) with `--memory-commit`.
- The central loop, run once by the main agent on the combined tree: `blaze check` then
  `blaze test`, keep-going (the default), every failure handed back with the tree, command and error.
- Run harnesses with `RUST_BACKTRACE=0`.
- Done: `blaze clean` in the worktree, `git worktree remove <dir>`, `ix rm <lane>`,
  `git branch -D <branch>` once merged.

# Changing code across blaze

<!-- Generated by `bun tools/agents/rules.ts --write` from tools/agents/rules.ts, down to the end marker; edit the rules there. AGENTS.md carries each rule as one line. -->

## fix-through-blaze-lints (rule 13)

A change that moves a type, path, API or idiom across the code is a ban with a `replacement` in
`.clippy.toml` (mirrored in the hot crates' `clippy.toml`), which blaze-lints'
`disallowed_types`/`disallowed_methods`/`disallowed_macros` enforce with a MachineApplicable fix, or
a `blaze::` lint where the rule needs types or MIR; either is applied with `blaze check --fix`, and
its count lives in `crates/blaze-lints/baselines/`, which may only shrink; a one-off move of a path
is `blaze check --replace A=B`. Both find code by name resolution (imports, renames, globs,
re-exports, macro output), never by text, and leave it compiling and lint-clean, so the rule keeps
holding after the port. `sed`, `rg` replace and syntax-only rewriters (astlog) are for syntax-only
shapes, scoped and checked by a build afterward.

## whole-ports (rule 24)

A change to a shared signature or type (a struct's fields, a trait, a lock type) updates every
caller in the same batch, so the shared tree compiles at every save point. Do it through `blaze
check --fix`, `blaze check --replace` or a scoped rewrite, then build, then hand the batch over. A
half-ported tree blocks every lane's run.

## best-long-term-design (rule 28)

Pick the best long-term design, not the least work: own the layer or port rustc's rule properly, and
spend the effort on proving it right: real crates' own test suites passing under blaze, Hegel
property tests and deterministic simulation of blaze's own invariants (`testing` skill), and fuzzing
of parsers of hostile bytes.

See [docs/contributing.md#rules-for-code](../../../docs/contributing.md#rules-for-code).

## spec-then-build (rule 29)

Before a change that spans crates, adds a concept, or changes a persisted format, a protocol or a
hot path, write a short spec as a `plan` doc under `docs/` (what, why, the chosen design and the
losing alternative in a line, the cost budget, the migration, how it is proven: for concurrent,
durable, billing or data-deleting code, the DST and the invariant its oracle checks). Have a fresh
reviewer check it against the code when it is large. Then start building it in the same lane, in the
same session, without waiting to be asked: fan out the code, build, land. The spec ships in the same
pull request as the first code that implements it, and is marked `current` (or rewritten to describe
what was built) once the work lands. A spec with no code behind it is unfinished work, not a result;
a lane that cannot build what it specified says what blocks it and who it handed the work to.

See [docs/contributing.md#rules-for-code](../../../docs/contributing.md#rules-for-code).

## one-concept-one-home (rule 30)

Each concept has one type, one rule and one place it is computed: two types for the same thing (a
`BuiltFor` in two crates), two copies of a rule (where code runs, what a key covers), two paths that
do the same job (two schedulers, two evaluators, two tiers for one level) are a bug. Merge them into
the better one, delete the other, and ban its name with a `replacement` (`fix-through-blaze-lints`);
a change that finds a duplicate removes it or files an issue naming both.

# Compiler correctness

<!-- Generated by `bun tools/agents/rules.ts --write` from tools/agents/rules.ts, down to the end marker; edit the rules there. AGENTS.md carries each rule as one line. -->

## no-rustc (rule 1)

blaze never runs rustc: no function, crate, std, build script, proc macro, test or link step goes to
rustc, rustdoc or a cargo that runs them. Each place that still does is a bug with a `no-rustc`
issue, to be removed, never extended.

See [docs/no-rustc.md](../../../docs/no-rustc.md).

## superset-of-rust (rule 4)

Own every layer from source to running code, never by narrowing what blaze accepts: every program
the pinned nightly builds must build and behave the same under blaze, with the real std, C
dependencies, build scripts and proc macros. The allowed differences are sandboxing and soundness:
where rustc accepts a program because of an objective bug in rustc (a soundness hole that lets safe
code cause undefined behavior, such as rust-lang/rust#25860, or another clear safety defect), blaze
refuses it with a hard error naming the hole, never by default copying the bug; a mere disagreement
with rustc's design is not such a bug. Superset means blaze may also accept more than Rust: an
extension (new syntax, attributes, semantics) only has to work under blaze, never under rustc, as
long as it is opt-in and every program that doesn't use it behaves exactly as under rustc.

See [docs/no-rustc.md](../../../docs/no-rustc.md).

## useful-not-parity (rule 5)

rustc and cargo are references, never specs. Judge everything blaze does by how useful it is to the
person or agent using it, not by how closely it matches them: errors, warnings, lints, CLI commands
and flags, printed and JSON output, progress, the target directory's layout, file formats, caches,
symbol names, debug info, what a build or test run does and in what order. Match them only where
real code or tools depend on it (a program's behavior, a published crate's manifest, an editor
reading the JSON); everywhere else pick the better design and delete the copy. Their style is no
constraint either: how cargo or rustc words, colours, lays out or orders a message, a progress line,
a summary or a flag is not a reason for blaze to do the same; design it as blaze would from scratch
(structured data first, rendered for a person on a terminal and as data for an agent) and change it
freely when a better way is found. Tests check what makes the result useful and correct, never that
it equals rustc's or cargo's. `superset-of-rust` is unchanged: every program the pinned nightly
builds still builds and runs as it does under rustc, except one that only builds through a rustc
soundness bug.

## blaze-uses-its-extensions (rule 6)

Only blaze builds blaze, so blaze's own source is blaze-only Rust: use its extensions
(`#[blaze::pure]`, `nopanic`/`noalloc`/`nonblocking`, `#[blaze::linear]`, contracts, comptime,
sealed traits) wherever they make blaze more correct or more incremental, and rely on them being
checked. No `cfg_attr` guard, no rustc-compatible copy, no inert-under-rustc fallback: an extension
blaze can't check yet is an error to fix in blaze. The one limit is stage 0: an extension blaze's
source uses must be one the stage-0 blaze (`.github/blaze-version`) already reads, so a new
extension lands in a release before blaze's source depends on it.

See [docs/future/bootstrap.md](../../../docs/future/bootstrap.md).

## sandbox-everything (rule 9)

Build scripts and proc macros always run sandboxed, on every platform; where no sandbox can be made,
blaze stops. Sandboxed tests are an opt-in experiment. The only ways out are the documented manifest
opt-outs and `BLAZE_SANDBOX=off`; nothing new that runs user code runs outside by default.

See [docs/cargo.md#build-scripts-and-proc-macros-run-in-a-sandbox](../../../docs/cargo.md#build-scripts-and-proc-macros-run-in-a-sandbox).

## proc-macros-on-wasm (rule 10)

A proc macro runs as a WebAssembly module: blaze compiles the macro crate to `wasm32-wasip1` with
its own front end and code generator (never rustc), and Wasmtime runs it in process, Cranelift as
its compiler, behind the `proc_macro` bridge, whose shims are its only imports. Cranelift's code
generator runs only there, inside Wasmtime for wasm. Native code (every target blaze builds for,
debug or release) is never generated by Cranelift: it is copy-and-patch stencils or LLVM, a function
with no stencil is a typed error naming it, and there is no Cranelift tier between them. Cranelift's
IR types (`cranelift_codegen::ir`) may stay as the stencils' input until blaze has its own IR. The
MIR evaluator stays for const eval and as the reference a macro's wasm output is tested against;
nothing hand-rolls a wasm-style sandbox (`blaze-macro-eval`'s `tier.rs` is replaced by this).

See [docs/v2/plan/lanes/usercode/macros.md](../../../docs/v2/plan/lanes/usercode/macros.md).

## keys-cover-every-input (rule 21)

A query key, store key, fold key or template key covers every input its value depends on, including
the data a constant points to and the identity of a closure callee. Two different values under one
key is a refusal with a typed error, never an overwrite, and the fix is the key, never the check.

## deterministic-output (rule 25)

No output (an object, a diagnostic's order, a store key, a profile row's identity) depends on
hash-map iteration order, thread timing, addresses or the wall clock. Hashers have fixed seeds,
except a table whose keys an attacker may pick (names, paths, literals), which is keyed by a
`blaze_hash::SipKey`: random when nothing persists its layout and nothing output depends on where a
key lands, or `blaze_ids::index_key` of its content when an image lays it out; a hot one may instead
be adaptive (`blaze_hash::adaptive`): the fixed hash until a lookup walks a run no honest keys make,
then a random `SipKey` for good. Anything iterated into output is sorted or ordered by construction;
a test builds twice and compares bytes.

## semantics-in-front-end (rule 31)

Language semantics (MIR building and passes, borrow checking, const eval, layout, code-identity
hashes) go in the front end's crates in `crates/` (`hir-ty`, `hir-def` and the rest, derived from
rust-analyzer but no longer synced with it), whose queries run on blaze's own engine
(`blaze_query::db`, crates/blaze-query: derived from salsa but not salsa; dense ids, in memory, one
view at a time; persisted, shared results go through blaze-kernel), in a crate of their own where
possible. Codegen, the store, the daemon, cargo integration and the runtime stay outside the front
end.

See [docs/contributing.md#where-new-code-goes](../../../docs/contributing.md#where-new-code-goes).

## library-over-language (rule 32)

Before adding an attribute, intrinsic or special case to the compiler, write the feature as library
code on what the language already has: traits, generics, const eval, compile-time reflection
(`core::mem::type_info`), allocators, effects and the purity proof. When it cannot be written that
way, the language is missing a primitive: add the smallest general one that makes the library
possible (nightly's API where one exists, otherwise an opt-in blaze extension), and keep the set of
primitives small. The compiler proves and exposes facts (purity, code identity, layout, reflection);
policy (caching, storage, hash formats, how code is executed) lives in libraries anyone can read or
replace. Example: `Canonical` is library code over `type_info`, and `#[blaze::cache]` lowers to a
call on a library `Executor`; the compiler generates neither the hashing nor the caching.

See [docs/contributing.md#where-new-code-goes](../../../docs/contributing.md#where-new-code-goes).

# Debugging blaze from its profile

<!-- Generated by `bun tools/agents/rules.ts --write` from tools/agents/rules.ts, down to the end marker; edit the rules there. AGENTS.md carries each rule as one line. -->

## ask-the-profile-first (rule 17)

Every daemon already records, per build, the footprint and live bytes, each task's granted and peak
memory, admission waits, spans and reruns, in `<BLAZE_HOME>/v2/profile/*.parquet`. A why question
(slow, rerunning, memory-hungry, idle workers) starts with `blaze explain footprint_per_build`,
`task_memory`, `admission_waits`, `worker_states` or a `blaze debug sql` query on the daemon that
showed it, and quotes the rows. A guess or a fresh experiment comes only after the rows can't
answer, and then the gap gets a span or counter.

<!-- End of the generated rules. Hand-written notes follow. -->

Every `blaze serve` daemon keeps a profile history: Parquet files that say what each build
ran, why, for how long and with how much memory. Answer "why" questions from those rows, not
from reading code and guessing. The schema is defined once, in
`crates/blaze-profile/src/schema.rs`, and documented column by column in `docs/profiling.md`.
This skill says how to read it and how to turn a reading into a proved cause.

Speed work also follows the `perf-and-tracing` rule (a span names the time before the fix).
This skill is the general method behind it, for reruns, memory and cycles too.

## The method

1. **Reproduce.** Find the smallest build that shows it: one edit, one command, one daemon.
   Write down the tree it ran on (commit and dirty diff; `builds.tree` and `builds.blaze` record
   it) so the claim names an exact tree (rule `measure-the-exact-tree`).
2. **Capture.** Run it under a daemon that keeps a history (any `blaze serve`). Use a fresh
   `BLAZE_HOME` per experiment so the build numbers are yours: `BLAZE_HOME=$(mktemp -d) blaze
   build`. Run the cold build, then the edit, then the warm build. Each build is a `build_id`.
3. **Query.** Start from counts (`query_counts`, `time_by_span_name`), then go to rows
   (`provenance`, `key_parts`, `spans`). Always filter by `build_id`.
4. **Claim.** State one cause and one effect in numbers taken from the rows: "`infer_query` ran
   4 120 times in build 3 because `FileText.text`(/src/lib.rs) changed, 3 900 of them through
   `item_tree`".
5. **Remove the cause and watch the effect go** (rule `test-the-cause`). Revert the edit, pin the
   input, or drop the untracked read; rerun the same steps on the same tree and quote the same
   query before and after. If the effect stays, the claim was wrong. Say so and go back to 3.

Never report a cause you have not removed. Never report a speedup that has no before and
after from the same query.

## Where the files are

- The history directory is `<state>/profile`. `<state>` is `$BLAZE_HOME/v2` when `BLAZE_HOME`
  is set, else `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/blaze/v2`, else `~/.cache/blaze/v2`.
- Each flush writes `<build>-<seq>.<table>.parquet` per table, and merges fold them into
  `<build>-<first>-<last>-<level>.<table>.parquet`. `manifest.json` lists the files that are
  the history, by table. A file on disk it does not list (a merge's retired input, held for a
  reader's pin) is not part of it: a glob over the directory can read rows twice. Every
  directory also holds an empty `schema.<table>.parquet` of each table, which has every column.
- `owner.lock` names the daemon that writes there.
- Files carry `blaze.schema` in their Arrow metadata. Schema 4 added `provenance` rows,
  `key_parts` and the `query_counts.ran_*` causes, and schema 5 `event_fields`. Older files read
  them as null.

## Running DuckDB

blaze never links DuckDB and never looks for it on `PATH`. `BLAZE_DUCKDB` names the binary as
an absolute path. `nix develop` sets it, and so does the installed `blaze` wrapper. Outside
both, run `nix run .#duckdb` (DuckDB 1.5.5, pinned in `flake.nix`) or set
`BLAZE_DUCKDB=$(nix build --no-link --print-out-paths .#duckdb)/bin/duckdb`.

- `blaze debug sql "<query>"` runs one query over the history with every table and view of
  `crates/blaze-profile/sql/views.sql` defined. `--json` prints rows as JSON for a script or a
  CI gate. It asks the daemon to flush first, so it sees every row recorded before it asked.
- `blaze explain <view> [name=value ...] [--json]` runs a named query from
  `crates/blaze-profile/sql/examples.sql`. With no arguments it lists them. Each view whose
  arguments all have defaults is also a DuckDB view of that name inside `blaze debug sql`, for
  the last build: `blaze debug sql "SELECT * FROM what_reran"`.
- `blaze slow [--build N]` is the one-screen answer to "what made it slow". `blaze why [ITEM]`
  says what the daemon computed again and why, item by item.
- For files outside a daemon (a CI artifact, another machine's home), call DuckDB directly on
  the files the manifest lists, never a glob: `files=$(jq -r '.tables.provenance // {} | keys |
  map("<dir>/" + .) | tojson' <dir>/manifest.json)`, then `$BLAZE_DUCKDB -c "SELECT ... FROM
  read_parquet($files, union_by_name = true)"`. A glob is right only for a copy of the
  directory with no retired files (the manifest's `retired` list empty).

## The tables that answer "why"

- `spans` has one row per span. `name` is the span kind (`unit bodies`, `macro expand`, `wait`,
  `task`, ...), and `function`, `crate`, `unit` and the typed columns say of what. A `task` span
  is one daemon plane task: `function` is its kind (`unit bodies (infer)`), plus `node`,
  `granted_bytes` (what memory admission granted, the predicted peak), `passed` (how many times
  another task started while its grant did not fit) and `peak_bytes` (the most it held). An
  `admission` span is the same task's wait from ready to start, with `awaits` saying what held
  it back: `memory`, `a work thread`, `an io thread` or `nothing` (null: it never started).
- `query_counts` has one row per query function per build, written always. `executed` and
  `verified` are runs and rows proved unchanged without running. `ran_new`, `ran_changed`,
  `ran_untracked`, `ran_cycle` and `evicted_asked` are the runs by cause and add up to
  `executed`; a mismatch is a bug in the engine. `written` is input writes, `reran` is runs
  in a view the row already ran in, and `reads_*` are read volume.
- `provenance` is the query engine's run log. It has one row per run that was not a first run,
  plus one row for each run's first untracked read. Columns: `query_key` (the query and its
  key as the key's `Debug` shows it, `` `infer_query`(DefWithBodyId(..)) ``), `kind`, `outcome`
  (`ran` or `untracked read`), `cause` (`changed`, `evicted`, `untracked`, `cycle`), `view`,
  `cause_key` (the read that changed: `` `FileText.text`(/src/lib.rs) `` for a file, another
  input's field by id, or another memo's `query_key`), `cause_kind` (`input`, `tracked`,
  `interned`, `function`) and `what` (the `Untracked { what }` name). Names are made only as
  the build ends, with its database, so logging stays cheap. It is written while the
  daemon keeps a history. Past 2^19 rows between two builds the rest are dropped with a
  `warn` event, and the counts still hold every run.
- `misses` has one row per unit, build-script run or codegen template that a build computed
  again, with the reason in words (`cause`, `what`, `was`, `now`, `since`). `blaze why` reads
  these rows.
- `key_parts` has one row per part of each miss's key: `step`, `item`, `key` (hex), `part`,
  `hash` (hex), `names` and `beyond`. Diff two builds with it, or two homes.
- `counters` holds time series: `live bytes`, `footprint bytes`, `pool queued`, and others.

## Ready queries

Each query below is a named view (`blaze explain <name>`) unless it says otherwise. Defaults:
`build` is the last build, `limit` is 20.

**Top time by span.** `blaze explain time_by_span_name build=N` gives time per span kind.
`blaze explain slowest_queries` lists the slowest query spans. For own CPU time by function:

```sql
SELECT name, function, count(*) AS spans, round(sum(self_cpu_ns) / 1e6, 1) AS self_cpu_ms
FROM spans WHERE build_id = 3
GROUP BY name, function ORDER BY self_cpu_ms DESC LIMIT 20
```

**What reran and why.**
- `blaze explain memo_hit_rate_per_query_kind build=N` gives, per query, how many runs were
  verified and how many ran, broken down by cause. Start here.
- `blaze explain what_reran build=N` lists each memo that ran again, with its cause and the read
  that changed.
- `blaze explain why_reran build=N` follows each rerun's `cause_key` through the memos that
  changed to the root (an input field, an untracked read, a cycle). It counts how many memos
  each root made run again, so the top row is usually the answer.
- `blaze explain untracked_reads build=N` lists the untracked reads by name. Each memo that made
  one reruns in every view, so a name here with many memos is a missing tracked input.
- To find what made one memo run, walk the chain by hand:

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
    SELECT query_key, cause, cause_key, cause_kind, 0 AS depth
    FROM provenance WHERE build_id = 3 AND query_key LIKE '`infer_query`(%my_fn%'
    UNION ALL
    SELECT p.query_key, p.cause, p.cause_key, p.cause_kind, chain.depth + 1
    FROM chain JOIN provenance p ON p.build_id = 3 AND p.query_key = chain.cause_key
    WHERE chain.cause_kind = 'function' AND chain.depth < 64
)
SELECT DISTINCT * FROM chain ORDER BY depth
```

- Units and build scripts: `blaze why`, or `SELECT step, item, cause, what FROM misses WHERE
  build_id = 3 AND cause <> 'first'`.

**Diffing two runs' keys.**
- `blaze explain key_part_diff after=M before=N` lists, for each thing build M computed again,
  each key part whose hash differs from the last build at or before N that computed it too.
- No rows while `misses` still says it missed means the key was the same. Look at `beyond`
  (process variables, traced reads) and at `misses.cause`.
- Across two homes, for example a cache miss on CI that you don't see locally:

```sql
WITH a AS (SELECT * FROM read_parquet('/tmp/home-a/v2/profile/*.key_parts.parquet', union_by_name = true) WHERE build_id = 2),
     b AS (SELECT * FROM read_parquet('/tmp/home-b/v2/profile/*.key_parts.parquet', union_by_name = true) WHERE build_id = 2)
SELECT coalesce(a.item, b.item) AS item, coalesce(a.part, b.part) AS part, a.hash AS a_hash, b.hash AS b_hash
FROM a FULL JOIN b ON a.step = b.step AND a.item = b.item AND a.part IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b.part
WHERE a.hash IS DISTINCT FROM b.hash ORDER BY item, part
```

  Run it with `$BLAZE_DUCKDB -c "..."`, on copies whose manifests retire nothing (else list the
  files from `manifest.json` as above). Build numbers differ across homes, so pick each side's
  build first.

**Memory by task.**
- `blaze explain task_memory build=N` shows, per task kind, the memory granted against the peak
  held, and how many tasks went over their grant. A kind that is often over its grant has a
  forecast that is too low.
- The whole-process line is the `live bytes` and `footprint bytes` counters
  (`blaze explain footprint_per_build`).
- Single tasks: `SELECT function, node, granted_bytes, peak_bytes FROM spans WHERE build_id = 3
  AND name = 'task' ORDER BY peak_bytes DESC NULLS LAST LIMIT 20`.

**Admission waits.**
- `blaze explain admission_waits build=N` gives, per task kind and what held it back (memory,
  a work or io thread, nothing), how many tasks waited, their whole and longest wait from ready
  to start, and how often memory passed them over.
- The longest single waits: `SELECT function, node, awaits, round(dur_ns / 1e6, 1) AS ms,
  passed FROM spans WHERE build_id = 3 AND name = 'admission' ORDER BY dur_ns DESC LIMIT 20`.
- Threads blocked inside tasks are `wait` spans: `SELECT awaits, waits_on, count(*),
  round(sum(dur_ns) / 1e6, 1) AS ms FROM spans WHERE build_id = 3 AND name = 'wait' GROUP BY
  ALL ORDER BY ms DESC`.
- `blaze explain uncovered_time` and `worker_states` say whether workers were idle while tasks
  waited.

**A cycle that won't settle.**
- `blaze explain cycle_reruns build=N` lists the memos that ran for a cycle, with their runs and
  views. One memo with many runs in one view is a cycle iterating.
- `SELECT kind, ran_cycle, executed FROM query_counts WHERE build_id = 3 AND ran_cycle > 0`
  gives the count per query.
- If the build never ends, `open` holds the spans every thread was inside at the last flush,
  and `blaze slow` reports a build whose daemon died.

## Limits to keep in mind

- A key's name is its `Debug`, which may still hold ids (`FunctionId(..)`) where the type
  prints no path, and an input other than a file's text is named by its id. Compare across
  daemons by query and count, or through `key_parts` and `misses`, which name items by path.
- The counts are process-wide (two overlapping builds share them); the run log is the front
  end's own.
- `admission` says memory only when the task was passed over for it; a wait behind another
  task's starvation hold reads as a thread.
- The `queries` view joins `provenance` on a span's `function`. That is a display name, so the
  join finds nothing. Read `provenance` directly.

## no-mcp (rule 33)

No MCP. Agent-facing interfaces are a Unix socket or HTTP with one versioned schema in deterministic

Every doc under `docs/` has front matter: `current` (kept true), `plan`, `record` (dated history) or
`superseded` (naming its replacement). Trust current docs; read plans and records as of their date.

A script takes one JSON value (a file path, `-` or inline), parsed into a frozen dataclass that

to this when next changed.

# Native UI as Flecs

General Flecs rules, traits and script syntax are in the `flecs` skill; this one is how the harness app builds UI
with them. Paths below are relative to `crates/harness/`. The app is copied from den's native stack: flecs v4.2.0
(the indexable-inc/flecs fork, branch `indexable/v4.2`, pinned by rev in `vendor/hyperion-flecs-c/Cargo.toml`; blaze's
`vendor/flecs-c` pins the same rev, and CI's `.github/scripts/flecs_pin.py` fails when they differ), Metal through the
indexable-inc/slang fork (`harness-native/build.rs`), den's text shaper plus Slug outlines, libghostty-vt for terminal
state (`harness-vt`).

## Layers (each knows only the ones below)

1. **Model** (`harness-native-model/src/lib.rs`): the world's domain. `Device` roots; `Object` entities with exclusive
   `(Kind, Claude|Codex|CursorAgent|Shell|Proc|Stage)` and `(Status, Running|Exited|Killed|Lost|Pending|Skipped)`,
   `Name`, `Title`, `Cwd`, `ExitCode`, `Created`/`Ended`, `Term`; runs carry `Run`, stages `StageNo`; flecs `ChildOf`
   for the tree; tags such as `Archived`, `Closed`, `Pinned`. The daemon feeds it (`DaemonInbox` system); auto-archive
   is the `ArchiveRule` system here.
2. **Primitives** (`harness-native-ui-prims/scene/prims.flecs` + the `harness-native-ui-{layout,motion,draw,input}`
   crates and their `-api` crates): the vocabulary every view is made of. Never draw ad hoc in Rust when a primitive
   (or a new one) fits.
3. **Views** (`harness-native/scene/10-harness.flecs`, `hn.*`): prefabs composed of primitives. Rust binds model to
   views by key with `harness_native_ui_view::for_each`/`for_each_of`/`lazy_for_each_of`.
4. **Tokens and theme** (`harness-native/scene/00-tokens.flecs`, `prefab hn.Theme` in 10-harness.flecs): every size,
   colour, radius and spring is an `export const` token; the user's Ghostty config (read by `harness-ghostty-config`,
   applied in `harness-native/src/app/ghostty.rs`) retints the theme-driven ones at runtime.
5. **Keys** (`harness-native/scene/20-keys.flecs`): bindings are data, see below.

Rust owns only: the terminal grid (thousands of cells a frame, never entities), key dispatch, the layout solver,
springs, drawing (shared with harness-video in `harness-native-render`: Metal, text, the paint pass), the daemon link. Everything a designer would tweak lives in script.

## The primitive vocabulary (SwiftUI's, as components)

| Want | Use |
| --- | --- |
| HStack / VStack / ZStack | `ui.Row`, `ui.Column`, `ui.ZStack` (`Flex: {axis, gap, align, justify, wrap}`) |
| Spacer, Divider | `ui.Spacer`, `ui.Divider` (`hn.Seam` for the 1pt vertical hairline) |
| .frame / .padding | `Size: {w, h}`, each axis `{kind: Fixed/Grow/Fit/Percent, value, min, max}`; `Padding: {l, r, t, b}`. Widths are proposals (SwiftUI's): a Fit node takes the less of its ideal width and the room, `max` is `.frame(maxWidth:)`, `FixedSize` is `.fixedSize()`; text wraps at what it gets (solve.rs's module doc) |
| Grid / LazyVGrid | `ui.Grid` + `ui.GridRow`/`ui.GridColumn`; `ui.AdaptiveGrid` with `GridColumns: {min, max}` |
| Long lists | `ui.LazyColumn`/`ui.LazyGrid` (`Lazy: {count, row, overscan}`) in a `ui.Scroll`: only visible rows exist (the Archive) |
| Words in a hugging plate (chat bubble, callout) | `ui.Bubble` (a Fit `ui.Box` capped by `Size.w.max`; its words wrap past it) |
| Text | `ui.Words` (wraps) / `ui.Line` / `ui.Lead` + `TextStyle`; `ui.LineMiddle`/`ui.LineHead` or `Truncate: {mode: Head/Middle/Tail}`; one line in rows, never wrap |
| Who truncates first | `ui.Lead` (`ShrinkFirst`), `LayoutPriority {value}`, `FixedSize {h, v}` (name truncates before badge) |
| Alignment | `Align: FirstBaseline/LastBaseline`, `AlignSelf`, `AlignmentGuide {dx, dy}` |
| Background / overlay | `Background` / `Overlay` tags on a child (laid to the parent's frame, out of flow); floating: `ui.Overlay` + `(AnchoredTo, node)` |
| Menu, popover, hover card past the window's edge | `Windowed` on the floating node (`ui.Menu`, `ui.Overlay`, `hn.GenFloat` carry it): its own borderless child window (`harness-native/src/window/overlay.rs`), placed and kept on the screen's visible frame (`Screen`), the system shadow under it; input stays in the main view's points. Toasts, sheets and dialogs over a pane stay in the window |
| Title-bar inset | `SafeAreaInset` / `SafeAreaPadding`, never hardcoded top padding |
| Responsive | `ui.ViewThatFits` (first child variant that fits) |
| Button / icon button | `ui.Button`; `ui.IconButton` (square wash hugging one `ui.Symbol`; never a full-width row wash) |
| Icons | `ui.Symbol` + `Icon: {glyph}` (den's icon set); `ui.Icon` + `Mark: {name}` for brand marks (vector, Slug) |
| Tooltip | `Tooltip: {text: "..."}` on any node (system tooltip; nearest ancestor's wins) |
| Pointer shape | `Cursor: {shape: Text}` on a node (nearest ancestor's wins; makes it a hit target): Text on what takes typing or selection, Arrow on controls, Hand only on links (macOS's conventions); the host's zones (terminal grid, sidebar edge) and drags in `harness-native/src/app/pointer.rs` |
| Scrolling | `ui.Scroll` (clips, shifts by `ScrollState`) carries `ui.Scroller`, macOS's overlay scroller: knob and track parts (`ScrollerPart`) layout places from `ScrollExtent`, motion fades and widens (`ScrollerState`), input drags and pages (`ScrollerGrip`); tokens `scroller_*`, `NoScroller` turns it off, `ScrollFed` lets a host feed the extent (the terminal), `scroll_quietly` moves without showing it. A host running its own physics (the tree's, harness-native-scroll-physics, in `harness-native/src/app/sidebar.rs`; a chat's) adopts a `ScrollState` the scroller wrote |
| Motion | `MatchedGeometry {id}` (selection pill), `Transition: {kind: Opacity/Slide/Scale/Move}`, `Animate`, `HoverAmt`/`HoverLift` springs; spring params are tokens |
| Pose / timeline | `Pose: {dx, dy, shrink, fade, cut}` (0 at rest; draw folds it into the subtree, layout ignores it); a `Cue` child animates any member by path over the clock (`harness-native-ui-timeline`, used by `harness-video`) |
| Text motion, code colour | `GlyphsIn: {at, per, dur, by, ease}` (glyph-by-glyph arrival), `Caret: {at, until, blink, ink}`, `Highlight: {file}` (tree-sitter, inks from `code_ink.<capture>` tokens). Words always break at the width their box has this frame, so they re-wrap live through a fold, instantly (only broken again over glyphs shaped once, `Layout::wrap`). Never lay words out at a rest width: `LaysAtRest` is for a terminal's grid only |
| Pixel art | `Picture: {handle}` + `Pixelated`, `Frames: {count, fps}` for a sheet; `BlazeMark: {start, exit}` for the live fire wordmark (`harness-native-blaze`). Drawn as one texture, texels fetched not filtered: never a panel per cell (those seam when scaled) |
| Clip | `Clip` (the sidebar fold lays out at full width and clips; never relayout at in-between widths) |

New UI need not covered here: add a primitive (component + prim prefab + a gallery example under
`harness-native-ui-prims/scene/examples/`), then use it. Gallery: `HARNESS_NATIVE_GALLERY=1` with `HARNESS_NATIVE_SHOT`.

## Today: prefabs filled from Rust

- Views are prefabs; Rust keeps rows by key with `for_each`/`for_each_of` (`ui.List` or a column) and
  `lazy_for_each`/`lazy_for_each_of` (a `Lazy` container), and sets what differs through `View::part("name")`
  (all in `harness-native-ui-view/src/lib.rs`).
- Write new views so they convert mechanically to the 4.2 style below: data in, parts derived from it.

## Flecs 4.2 traps (the vendored version)

- The 4.2 changes (explicit deferral, `Copy`, Parent storage) are in the `flecs` skill. Here: mutate from systems
  through the stage (`vendor/hyperion-ecs/src/system.rs`: `Iter::world` and the stage accessor) or collect, then write;
  never rely on implicit `defer_begin`.
- Script prefab/template children default to Parent storage in 4.2. The shutdown abort it caused
  (flecs_non_fragmenting_childof_move) is fixed in the fork (upstream flecs#2384), but the views still find children
  through ChildOf tables (without `@tree ChildOf` the window draws empty), so each top-level scene scope keeps
  `@tree ChildOf` until they read Parent children too.
- Since 4.2, prefabs, constraint traits, cached queries and query plans are addons: features of `hyperion-flecs-c`.
- flecs orders the systems of one phase by entity id, not by when they were made (a scene load recycles ids), so a
  system that must see another's results in the same `progress` goes in a later `Phase` (harness-native-flecs: the
  layout pass in `Layout`, hits and matched geometry in `AfterLayout`, the pointer's resolve in `Resolve`, the draw pass
  in `Draw`) and declares what it `reads`/`writes` so flecs merges first. Zoom is a uniform scale: layout, draw and input
  are in view points (window points over `App::zoom()`), plates snap to device pixels at rest, and matched geometry lands
  (never slides) when the room changes.

## Target: reactive templates (4.2 has them; no view uses them yet)

Views are being converted from the prefab style above; write new keyed views as templates once the conversion lands.
A row/pane/overlay is a `template` whose `prop`s are its data; conditional parts are `if` blocks. Fine-grained
reactivity re-runs only the statements that read a changed prop, and children survive, so springs, hover and
matched-geometry state on them keep running.

```
template hn.ObjRow {
  prop name = ""
  prop kind = Kind.Shell
  prop depth = 0
  prop code = 0
  prop folded = false
  prop has_children = false

  ui.Row { Padding: {l: depth * $indent} }
  if has_children { chevron : hn.Disclosure { Rotation: {deg: match folded { true: 0; false: 90 }} } }
  icon : ui.Icon { Mark: {name: kind_mark(kind)} }   // fn kind_mark in script
  label : ui.Lead { Text: {s: name} }
  if code != 0 { badge : hn.Badge { Text: {s: "{code}"} } }

  async {                                             // small behaviour lives with the widget
    while true { await on.activate(this); folded = !folded }   // flecs.script.input has no double-click
  }
}
```

- Rust sets the instance's props from the model (one `set` per changed row) and never pokes `part("...")`.
- Use template interfaces for families (an interface struct `Row`, `template SessionRow : Row`), and pass a
  template as a prop (`prop row: template Row`) to share list code between sidebar and archive.
- The language itself (props, muts, interfaces, `for`, `fn`, `include`, string formats, vectors, maps, `export mut`
  tokens Rust may change, async and input events) is the `flecs` skill's `script.md`.
- `async` + `flecs.script.input` must be bridged to our pointer/key system; if a behaviour needs the hot path
  (terminal input, key dispatch), keep it in Rust.

## Tokens, theme and look

- One theme: every colour is a role at the top of 00-tokens.flecs (`tone_<role>`, the blaze site's palette, dark and
  light): grounds `ground`, `sidebar`, `card`, `raised` (menus, popovers), `well` (fields, code), `term_ground`; lines
  `line`, `line_strong`; inks `ink_strong`, `ink`, `ink_muted`, `ink_faint`; washes `hover`, `wash`, `selection`,
  `selection_focus`, `press`, `scrim`; `accent`, `accent_wash`, `on_accent`, `link`, `code_ink`; states `success`,
  `warning`, `error` and their `_wash`. Below them sit the palettes (kinds, brand marks, file types, chart series,
  GitHub states, `code_ink.*`), colours that name a thing. A widget names a role (`Fill: $tone_card`), never a colour,
  and never a new one-off token: add a role if none fits. `no_raw_colours` (harness-native's app.rs tests) fails on a
  colour literal elsewhere; harness-video/scene/tokens.flecs mirrors the roles in its own look.
- Sizes, radii and springs are `export const` tokens in 00-tokens.flecs too, never literals in a view.
- Colour, size and spring roles come from `hn.Theme` children (`hn.Theme.card` reads `$tone_card`: a token named like
  the entity that reads it does not resolve, flecs#2389); Rust reads them by name (`harness-native/src/look.rs` `role`,
  `tone`) and panics on a missing one.
- The sidebar is the main card's own ground with one `line` hairline (hn.Seam) between them: no lighter slab, no
  shadow. Only the terminal follows the user's Ghostty theme: its palette, cursor, font, padding and `term_ground` (a
  terminal pane's ground, src/app/ghostty.rs); the app's chrome stays the theme's.
- Taste: native macOS, minimal. One font family for UI (Inter) at macOS sizes, hierarchy by weight/size/tone,
  no noise on rows, meta on hover, highlights hug their target, motion on springs, never a step.

## Keybindings are data

`harness-native/scene/20-keys.flecs`: `act.*` action entities (params such as `SpawnKind`, `ZoomStep`, `SelectN`,
`Bytes` on `act.SendBytes` children; `MenuItem`, `Selector`), `key.* { Keybind: {key, cmd, shift, opt, ctrl};
(Does, act.X); (When, ctx.Tree) }`. No `When` holds everywhere; the innermost active context wins (`ctx.Palette` or `ctx.Picker`,
`ctx.Archive`, then `ctx.Tree` over `ctx.Terminal`), later bindings win, unbound keys go to the terminal. The menu bar,
palette hints and sidebar cmd+1-9 hints are generated from the same entities. User overrides:
`$HARNESS_HOME/keys.flecs` (default `~/.harness`), run after the scene, reloaded when it changes. A new binding to an
existing action is entities only; a new action also needs a handler under its name in `harness-native/src/app/keys.rs`.

## Verify (no focus-taking, ever)

- First, after any `.flecs` change: `CARGO_TARGET_DIR=target cargo test -p harness-native scenes_load` (from
  `crates/harness/`). It builds the world headless (no window, Metal or daemon), loads every scene script (tokens, prims,
  the harness scene and its widgets, keys, the prims gallery and every example) and fails with flecs's error and line. A
  scene that does not load (a prefab named like a component it sets, an entity named by a script keyword such as `new`,
  an unknown token) otherwise only shows at launch, as an empty window. Run it before every push.
- Offscreen: `HARNESS_NATIVE_SHOT=out.png HARNESS_NATIVE_SHOT_SECS=2` (default 2.5; + `HARNESS_NATIVE_SHOT_HOVER=x,y,t`
  in window points, `HARNESS_NATIVE_SHOT_KEY=k,t`, `HARNESS_NATIVE_SHOT_SEQ=t0,t1` for frame sequences,
  `HARNESS_NATIVE_SIDEBAR=0`, `HARNESS_NATIVE_APPEARANCE=light`); see `harness-native/src/shot.rs` for the rest.
- A real window without activation: `HARNESS_NATIVE_NO_ACTIVATE=1`. Never activate windows or synthesize input
  on the user's machine; use a private `HARNESS_HOME` daemon for tests.
- The system pointer isn't in shots: `HARNESS_NATIVE_CURSOR_LOG=1` logs each shape change, a shot's hovers (`x,y,t;x,y,t`) log
  theirs, F3's `ptr` line shows it; `HARNESS_NATIVE_GALLERY=prims` draws one of every primitive.
- F3 shows the stats overlay (fps, cpu/gpu frame times, redraw reason, entity/draw counts); with nothing moving its
  state line must read idle.
- Read the shot (or a 2x crop) before saying a visual change is done; measure alignment in pixels.

# Flecs

General Flecs first, then the site. Building native UI out of Flecs (the harness app, `crates/harness`) is the
`flecs-ui` skill; it uses the language described here. Script language reference: `script.md`.

Sources, in order of trust: harness's v4.2.0 `distr/flecs.{h,c}` (the indexable-inc/flecs fork at the rev in `crates/harness/vendor/hyperion-flecs-c/Cargo.toml`; after a build, cargo's checkout of it is under `~/.cargo/git/checkouts/flecs-*`), the upstream v4.2.0 docs
(`docs/FlecsScript.md`, `ComponentTraits.md`, `HierarchiesManual.md`, `Systems.md` at tag v4.2.0; flecs.dev serves
master), then blog posts never. The "needs 4.2" marks here and in `script.md` were checked on 2026-11-03 by running
small scripts through each build listed below.

## Which Flecs runs where

| Runtime | Flecs | Pinned in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| harness native app | v4.2.0 (fork `indexable-inc/flecs`, branch `indexable/v4.2`) | `flecs-distr` rev in `crates/harness/vendor/hyperion-flecs-c/Cargo.toml` |
| blaze daemon's build page (`crates/blaze-web`, through `vendor/flecs-c`) | the same v4.2.0 fork rev as harness | `flecs-distr` rev in `vendor/flecs-c/Cargo.toml`; `.github/scripts/flecs_pin.py` (CI's `changes` job) fails if it differs from harness's |
| site build (`site-snapshot.wasm`) | upstream master `785ea7c` (2026-10-15, 90 commits before v4.2.0); its header says 4.1.6. Addons: SCRIPT, PREFAB, LOG only | flecs-opinionated rev in `site/renderer/Cargo.toml` |
| site type checker (`flecs-doc.wasm`) | `v4.1.6-665-gce3b06a6e`; accepted and rejected the same scripts as `785ea7c` | `site/flecs/FLECS_VERSION` |

The site is not on the shared pin: its runtime is flecs-opinionated's `flecs-c`, whose own vendored flecs is still
pre-4.2 (main at upstream `37a7ef90d` on 2026-11-04). Moving it means porting flecs-opinionated to 4.2, then the
site's `.flecs` files (`Override` to `Copy` and the rest of `script.md`'s **4.2** marks) and rebuilding `flecs-doc.wasm`.

"v4.1.6" on the site means the header, not the release: the v4.1.6 tag's script language is older (it rejects
`struct P(x: f32)`, typed `prop`, `match`, vector literals, maps, `export mut`). Never write site script from 4.1.6-era
docs. Use the 4.2 language and avoid what `script.md` marks **4.2**.

## Rules

- **Component-wise design.** One small component per concern, a tag for a bit of state, a pair for a link. An entity
  is the set of components it carries, and readers dispatch on them.
- **Prefabs for shared shape.** A prefab carries what every instance shares, and an instance overrides by setting its
  own value. By default `OnInstantiate` copies: on 4.2 it is called `Copy`; before 4.2, and on the site, it was
  `Override`. Exclusive relationships replace, so `(Status, Discussing)` on an instance replaces the prefab's
  `(Status, Draft)`.
- **Split a value where instances differ.** A component written in script sets every member (members left out are 0),
  so one component mixing per-instance members with shared ones makes every instance restate all of them. Give each
  concern its own component so the prefab holds the defaults and an instance writes only what differs (harness-video's
  sounds: `Sound {voice}`, `Onset {at}`, `Lasts`, `Pitch`, `Gain`, `Pan` on the `sound.*` prefabs, `src/sound.flecs`;
  `ding : sound.Bell { Onset: {at: 2.0} }` takes the rest from the prefab). Ship shared prefabs once, in a script the
  host loads before every scene, never copied into each scene. Reach for a template only when its body computes from
  its props.
- **Relationships, not strings, for links.** `(DependsOn, x)`: an unknown target fails the script at once.
- **Traits before first use.** Declare a trait right after the type, before any entity uses it. Symmetric,
  PairIsTag and Final abort if added late.
- **Child order needs `OrderedChildren`** on the parent. Without it, `ecs_children` returns table order, not script
  order (queries ignore it either way).
- **Never persist a raw entity id.** Ids differ between runs; persist paths.
- **Script declares; it does not sort or query.** Ordering belongs to whoever reads the world: put the key in a
  component and sort on it (path as tie-breaker), or use a query with `order_by` (cached queries keep the sort) or
  `group_by`. Use child order only for things whose order is written in one place (the blocks of one page).

## Traits (details: `docs/ComponentTraits.md` at v4.2.0)

| Trait | Say it when | Gotcha |
|---|---|---|
| `Exclusive` | a relationship holds one target per entity (one-of state, owner, parent) | add replaces; fires OnRemove for the old pair then OnAdd for the new |
| `Symmetric` | `R(a,b)` implies `R(b,a)` (peer, adjacent) | declare before any use (aborts); needs both ends alive |
| `Transitive` | `R(a,b), R(b,c)` implies `R(a,c)` in queries (LocatedIn) | query-time only; implies Traversable and Acyclic |
| `Reflexive` | `R(x,x)` is true for every x (IsA-like) | only changes query answers |
| `Acyclic` / `Traversable` | the relation is a DAG and queries traverse it with `up`/`cascade` | cycles are not reliably detected |
| `OneOf` | the target must be a child of an enum entity (`(Mode, Dark)`) | violation aborts at add |
| `With` | adding A must also add B | the only trait allowed after a query exists |
| `Relationship` / `Target` / `Trait` | entity may only be used as relationship / target / trait | misuse panics |
| `PairIsTag` | a pair never carries data, even when the target is a component | declare before use |
| `Final` | no entity may `IsA` this component | aborts if already inherited from |
| `Inheritable` | the component may be an `IsA` target and queries honour it | opt-in; tags inherit anyway |
| `OnInstantiate` `Copy` / `Inherit` / `DontInherit` | how a prefab's component reaches instances (copy / share / skip) | default `Copy`; named `Override` before 4.2 (the site) |
| `Sparse` | stable pointers, cheap add/remove, no row move | slower iteration |
| `DontFragment` | very sparse pair or component, avoids a table per target | no `target_for`, no Or/Optional/AndFrom/NotFrom, no inheritance, no monitors |
| `CanToggle` | enable/disable without a table move, value kept | small query overhead for all |
| `Singleton` | one value per world, stored on the component entity | cannot be added to other entities |
| `OrderedChildren` (on a parent) | children keep creation or custom order | `ecs_set_child_order` aborts on a wrong set |
| `OnDelete` / `OnDeleteTarget` + `Remove` / `Delete` / `Panic` | what happens to users of an entity that is deleted | default Remove (tags, pairs), Panic (components); `ChildOf` is `OnDeleteTarget Delete` |

Built-in implications: Traversable implies Acyclic; Transitive implies Traversable; DontFragment implies Sparse;
Module implies Singleton. `ChildOf`, `OnDelete`, `OnDeleteTarget`, `OnInstantiate` are Exclusive. `IsA`, `ChildOf`,
`SlotOf`, `DependsOn`, `With` are PairIsTag. In a 4.2 custom build, Acyclic, Final, OneOf, Relationship, Singleton,
Symmetric, Target and Trait need the `FLECS_CONSTRAINT_TRAITS` addon.

## Hierarchies: ChildOf and Parent storage (4.2)

- `ChildOf` (a pair) puts each parent's children in their own table. `Parent` (a component whose value is the parent,
  plus an automatic `(ParentDepth, @n)` pair) keeps children of many parents in one table. That makes prefab
  instantiation cheap (no new tables, a cached "TreeSpawner"), but deleting one child is O(n) in its siblings, and
  queries that mix a `ChildOf` term with others get slower. See `HierarchiesManual.md`, "Hierarchy storage".
- In script, plain scopes use `ChildOf`. On 4.2, **children of prefabs and templates default to `Parent`**, and
  instance children of a `Parent` prefab come out unnamed (`#493`, not `inst.kid`). Write `@tree ChildOf` before
  the `prefab`/`template` to keep names and `ChildOf`; `@tree Parent` opts a plain scope in. Before 4.2 (the site),
  prefab and template children use `ChildOf`.

## Flecs 4.2 C API changes (for binding and system code)

- **Explicit deferral.** In `ecs_iter_t`, `it->world` is the real world and `it->stage` the deferred one; v4.1.6 had
  `it->world` (maybe a stage) and `it->real_world`. In a normal (readonly) system a structural change through
  `it->world` asserts (`EcsWorldReadonly`); pass `it->stage` to queue it. In an `immediate` system `it->world` applies
  at once and `it->stage` still queues. C++: `it.stage()`, `it.world()`, `e.stage(it.world())`.
- `(OnInstantiate, Override)` is `(OnInstantiate, Copy)`: `EcsOverride` no longer exists.
- `ecs_entity_desc_t` lost `add`, `set` and `add_expr`; give a system its phase with `ecs_system_desc_t.phase`.
- Prefabs, constraint traits, cached queries and query plans are now addons (`FLECS_PREFAB`,
  `FLECS_CONSTRAINT_TRAITS`, `FLECS_CACHED_QUERIES`, `FLECS_QUERY_PLANS`); a `FLECS_CUSTOM_BUILD` must name them.
  New script addons: `FLECS_SCRIPT_ASYNC`, `FLECS_SCRIPT_INPUT` (was `FLECS_SCRIPT_EVENT` before the release),
  `FLECS_SCRIPT_SHELL`, `FLECS_SCRIPT_PLATFORM`, `FLECS_SCRIPT_MATH`.

## The site (runtime labelled v4.1.6; see the table above)

### Where Flecs runs

- **Pages are scripts.** `site/content/schema.flecs` defines the element types (structs such as `P`, `Li`, `Code`,
  `Section`, `Issue`; container tags `Ul`, `Ol`, `Table`, `Tr`; widget tags `RfcIndex`, `References`, `Course`,
  `UpdateLog`, `BenchHistory`), the relationships (`Status`, `Cites`, `DependsOn`, and the course graph's `Requires`
  and `InTheme`) and the page prefabs (`Page`, `Doc : Page`, `Rfc : Doc`). `refs.flecs` holds `Ref` entities. Every
  other file adds pages under `site { ... }`; entity paths are URLs (`site.rfcs.capabilities` is `/rfcs/capabilities`,
  `site.index` is `/`).
- **Order:** `schema.flecs`, `refs.flecs`, then the rest in path order, all in one world (`site/gen/build.ts`). Names
  reopen across files, so `site { rfcs { x : Rfc {...} } }` in its own file adds a child to the existing `rfcs`.
- **The build runtime** is `site-snapshot.wasm` (`site/renderer/snapshot`): Flecs's C compiled in through
  flecs-opinionated's `flecs-c` (wasm32-unknown-unknown, no WASI). `gen/build.ts` runs each script once with
  `ecs_script_run` (unmanaged: no reactivity, no async) and gets a DAG-CBOR snapshot (`.gen/site.cbor`) of every entity
  under the roots. Rust modules are built on a dev host or in CI and fetched with `renderer/fetch.py`; see
  `site/renderer/README.md`.
- **The renderer** is `site.wasm` (`site/renderer/core`, Rust, no Flecs inside): `world.rs` is the entity store loaded
  from the snapshot (prefab values merged, nearest wins), `render.rs` maps each element type to HTML and builds the
  widgets. The build renders static pages with it, the worker renders comment pages per request with the same module.
  A node with no known element type fails the build with its path.
- **The type checker** (`site/flecs-mapper`, TS 7.1 content mapper) runs scripts in `site/flecs/flecs-doc.wasm`
  (`flecs-doc.c` plus amalgamated Flecs, wasm32-wasi, built by `site/flecs/build.py`). A script must pass both.

### Site conventions

- `Page`, `Doc`, `Rfc` carry what every instance shares (`OrderedChildren`, `Discussable`, `(Status, Draft)`).
  Every container type gets `(With, flecs.core.OrderedChildren)`, and a new container type needs the same line.
- Links are pairs: `(Cites, refs.koka)`, `(DependsOn, site.charter)`. Inline `[[name]]` references are checked by the
  renderer instead.
- **Names are anchors.** In a `Doc` (anything people comment on), every block needs a name: its path under the page
  is the comment anchor (`motivation.why`). Renaming or moving a block orphans its comments (they still show, under
  the page discussion, with their quote). Choose names that describe the content, not its position.
- **Sort by data across files.** Child order is creation order, and across files that depends on file names and
  forward references: naming `site.rfcs.x` in a pair, or opening `x {}` early, creates `x` at that point (RFC 0003
  opening `"linear-types" {}` once made the index read 0001, 0003, 0002). Sorted things carry a key (`Number` on an
  `Rfc`, `order` on `Nav` and `Link`); the renderer sorts in `World::rfcs(parent)` and the nav.

### Gotchas found building the site

- A prefab body cannot name an entity defined later (`(DependsOn, site.charter)` in `Rfc` fails in schema.flecs,
  which runs first). Put such pairs on instances.
- Kind syntax `P why("...")` is `why { P: {"..."} }`. `Tag name` works for tags (`RfcIndex list`).
- Script errors print `file: line: message` with the source line; the build stops.
- String escapes, reserved words and the rest of the language traps: `script.md`, "Traps".

# Landing changes

<!-- Generated by `bun tools/agents/rules.ts --write` from tools/agents/rules.ts, down to the end marker; edit the rules there. AGENTS.md carries each rule as one line. -->

## land-through-pr (rule 37)

Land small and often through a pull request: `python3 .github/scripts/land.py "what the branch
does"` opens it, turns on auto-merge and waits for the merge gate (`--wait` resumes). Harnesses run
after merge in the release train. Never push to main.

See [docs/contributing.md#landing-a-change](../../../docs/contributing.md#landing-a-change).

## own-prs-to-merge (rule 38)

Any agent may take any open pull request or issue to done (merge main, resolve conflicts, fix its
gate, finish a draft) rather than hand it back; tell the owning lane what changed. Close one only
when it is wrong, saying why.

## credit-people (rule 40)

A commit or pull request built on someone's suggestion, diagnosis or patch gets a `Co-authored-by:
Name <id+login@users.noreply.github.com>` trailer for each of them and says where it came from.

See [docs/contributing.md#credit](../../../docs/contributing.md#credit).

## How landing works

From [docs/contributing.md#landing-a-change](../../../docs/contributing.md#landing-a-change):
`land.py` pushes the branch, opens "Merge <branch>: what the branch does" and turns on auto-merge.
The merge gate is the build and unit tests on Linux AArch64 (ix runners) and the released blaze's
`blaze check --workspace` on Linux AArch64 and macOS, with astlog's rules and the lint baselines.
There is no merge queue; the release train on main catches changes that break together. The wait
runs in its own process, logging to `.git/land/pr-N.log` in the main checkout; `land.py --wait`
follows it again. A branch that conflicts gets `git merge origin/main` first. For anything the
fast tier does not cover, run the train on the branch first: `gh workflow run train.yaml --ref <branch>`.

A `Co-authored-by:` trailer uses the address the person's own commits use, or
`<id>+<login>@users.noreply.github.com` with the id from `gh api users/<login> -q .id`; name the
issue or comment the idea came from in the message too, and keep every trailer through a squash.

## slow-is-p0-traced (rule 16)

Anything slow is a P0 until a span names it, and the trace comes before the speed fix. Every stretch
of worker time sits under a `tracing::info_span!(target: "blaze", ...)` that names the work: the

# Writing blaze's runtime code

<!-- Generated by `bun tools/agents/rules.ts --write` from tools/agents/rules.ts, down to the end marker; edit the rules there. AGENTS.md carries each rule as one line. -->

## no-fallback (rule 3)

No fallback, ever. When blaze can't do something it stops with an error naming what and where, never
quietly takes another path (rustc, a full link or rebuild instead of a patch, a slower backend, an
older cached result, a default guessed for a missing value). A fallback that only logs its reason is
still a fallback. A change that touches an existing fallback turns it into an error, and a bench or
test that hits one fails instead of timing the slow path.

## bump-allocate (rule 11)

Allocate by lifetime, never from the global heap by default: a collection that lives within one task
(a query run, a codegen unit, a maintainer pass) names its allocator, `Vec::new_in(frame)` /
`Box::new_in(.., frame)` from `blaze_mem::frame::current`, and longer lifetimes use the request,
revision or image allocator. A global allocation (`Vec::new`, `vec![]`, `collect` into a heap `Vec`,
`Box::new`, `to_owned`) needs `// alloc: <why>` on its line. `blaze::implicit_allocator` enforces
this, warning everywhere and denied wherever `blaze::hot` is, with `blaze::hot_alloc` for what a
call reaches.

See [docs/v2/plan/design/memory.md](../../../docs/v2/plan/design/memory.md).

## standard-structures (rule 12)

One choice per need, never a hand-rolled or std stand-in: a lock is `blaze_core::lock::{Lock,
ReadLock}` (with `Signal` for a driver thread's condition), named where it is made
(`Lock::new("store.packs", v)`), held only for a field update and never across a query call, IO or a
global allocation (`blaze::lock_held_across_slow`); raw `std::sync` and `parking_lot` locks are
banned in `.clippy.toml` outside `crates/blaze-core/src/lock.rs`, and a contended wait records who
waited behind whom into the profile's `lock_waits` (`blaze debug locks` ranks them and says what to
use instead: arc-swap or RCU for reads, papaya for a map, an atomic for an integer, a channel for a
queue, an owner for one holder); a shared map is `papaya::HashMap`; a single-owner map or set is
`blaze_hash::{HashMap<K, V, A>, HashSet<K, A>}` (foldhash with a fixed seed, its allocator named: a
frame's for a task, `Global` with a reason otherwise), with `blaze_hash::KeyHasher` for keys that
are already content hashes and `blaze_hash::Blake3Hasher` for persisted content IDs; results of
parallel items come back from `blaze_graph::par` in order, never pushed into a `Mutex<Vec>`; a queue
is `crossbeam::queue::{SegQueue, ArrayQueue}`; a channel is `crossbeam-channel`; a counter or flag
is an atomic. How a thread or fiber waits is `deadline-waits`. `BTreeMap` only where iteration order
is part of the output.

## sans-io-cores (rule 14)

Every core (a scheduler decision, a protocol, a retry or backoff policy, a lease, a maintainer's
plan) is a synchronous state machine that reads time only from an injected clock
(`advance_clock(now)`), owns no socket, file, thread, timer or sleep, and hands back decisions and
deadlines (`take_decisions`, `next_deadline`). Drivers do the IO and stay thin. A test replays a
transcript with no real clock, and a deterministic simulation test drives the core through
`blaze_core::sim::Sim` (`testing` skill): a core that does its own IO cannot be simulated, so it
cannot be proven. Protocol code is a core too: an HTTP client or server, TLS (through rustls's own
byte-in/byte-out `Connection`, never `tokio-rustls`), the daemon's wire protocol, a remote-cache or
registry client. Its interface is bytes in, bytes and events out, so any IO backend can drive it
(tokio today, io_uring on Linux later) by writing one thin driver, with no change to the core. A
dependency that ties protocol logic to one runtime (hyper's connectors, hyper-util, reqwest,
tokio-rustls) is replaced by a core and a driver, not wrapped. Persisted state is a core too: a
writer of files that must survive a crash (a manifest, a journal, a history, a store) asks for each
write, sync, rename, delete and lock as a blaze-core `Effect` and takes `Completion`s, so `Sim` sees
every one and can tear what was not synced; its durability is the order of the effects it emits,
never a direct `fsync`, `F_FULLFSYNC` or `flock`. Each core module carries `#![blaze::sans_io]` and
`#![deny(blaze::sans_io_core)]`: the lint walks every call the module makes, through workspace
functions, and refuses the clock, `std::fs`, `std::thread`, `std::net`, `std::process`, `std::env`,
OS randomness and `libc`/`rustix`/`nix`. What a core needs of its process beyond IO (its pid,
whether another process lives, symbols to name a stack) comes through a trait the driver implements,
taken as a type parameter: calls through it are the driver's, not the core's. Drivers are separate,
unmarked modules, so the exemption is by module, never by an allow on a line. A core's errors carry
the path the driver will report, and a step that waits on no effect is a typed error
(`bounded-progress`).

## every-wait-says-what (rule 15)

A thread or fiber that blocks says what it waits for: the wait opens a span naming the awaited key,
lock, channel, IO or child, and its owner when known. A wait with no name, and time on a worker
covered by no span, are bugs; the profile test fails on them.

## bounded-progress (rule 18)

Every loop that waits for progress (a solver, a fixpoint, a readiness probe, a retry) has a bound
(fuel, depth or a deadline from the injected clock) and ends in a typed outcome: done, or a failure
naming what it was doing, the goal or key, and how far it got. Never an open loop whose only exit is
success, and never a spin with no cap.

## errors-name-the-thing (rule 19)

An error names the item it is about (the function or instance with its path, the crate, the key, the
file and line) and the rule that refused it, in the message itself. "a template made against 6
references is given 7" is unfinished until it says which function and which template.

## panics-fail-one-job (rule 20)

A panic inside a job (a query, a codegen unit, a proc-macro evaluation) fails that job's units with
a typed error naming the panic and the job; the daemon keeps serving and keep-going (the default;
`--fail-fast` opts out) keeps building the rest. Formatting an error must not panic: render what
needs the database while the database is attached.

## no-wait-across-thread-locals (rule 27)

A fiber can resume on another thread after any wait, so nothing held across a wait may be tied to a
thread: no thread-local borrow, lock guard or `Rc`. Mark regions that must not wait with `NoWait`;
read thread-locals in `#[inline(never)]` functions that end before any wait.

## deadline-waits (rule 44)

A thread blocks in the kernel only through `blaze_core::wait`, which takes an absolute `Deadline` on
the injected clock (a driver's `now()`), recomputes the time left from that clock before every
system call, treats an interrupted (EINTR) or spurious return as a retry, and ends in a typed
outcome (`Waited::Ready` or `Waited::Deadline`), with fuel for a clock that does not move.
`Driver::poll` takes that `Deadline`, never a relative timeout, so no layer restarts one. The
kernel's waits (`poll`, `ppoll`, `select`, `epoll_wait`, `kevent`, `nanosleep`, `usleep`, `sleep`,
`GetQueuedCompletionStatusEx`, ...) are banned in `.clippy.toml` outside
`crates/blaze-core/src/wait*`, each with its `blaze_core::wait` replacement; io_uring waits pass a
signal mask that blocks every asynchronous signal but the stop signals. Only IO driver threads and
the pool's idle park block in the kernel: a fiber that waits, with a deadline or without, parks on
the scheduler (a key, a counter, a job, a timer on the driver's wheel), never a `Condvar`, a channel
receive, `thread::sleep` or a raw `spin_loop`; elsewhere a spin is the one bounded spin-then-park
helper. Nothing sends a signal to a pool or driver thread: the sampler reads the kernel's samples
(Linux `perf_event_open`) or stops the thread (macOS `thread_suspend`, Windows `SuspendThread`). The
DST in `crates/blaze-core/src/wait/tests.rs` interrupts every wait and checks that it ends by its
deadline, with a planted relative-timeout retry it must catch.

See [docs/v2/plan/design/deadline-waits.md](../../../docs/v2/plan/design/deadline-waits.md).

## macos-private-apis (rule 45)

On macOS, use any private or undocumented interface (Mach calls, libsystem and libdispatch
internals, `__ulock_wait2`, `kevent_qos`/`kevent_id` workloops, `sandbox_init_with_parameters`,
kperf, `thread_selfcounts`, `proc_info`, ...) where it is more efficient or more capable than the
public one, and the public one where it is the better (`os_sync_wait_on_address_with_deadline`'s
absolute deadline over `__ulock_wait2`'s relative one). Each use carries a comment naming the symbol

# Testing blaze

<!-- Generated by `bun tools/agents/rules.ts --write` from tools/agents/rules.ts, down to the end marker; edit the rules there. AGENTS.md carries each rule as one line. -->

## test-the-cause (rule 23)

A causal claim (this change caused the regression, this lock causes the convoy, this index makes it
fast) is tested by removing the cause and watching the effect go, not by checking that its premises
hold. Pin a load-bearing one with a test named for the property.

## persisted-state-round-trips (rule 26)

Anything blaze persists (the daemon image, the store, the plane's history) has a test that restores
it and checks the result equals a fresh build byte for byte, and a budget for restart to first
answer. A restore that silently starts empty is a failure the daemon reports, naming why. A format
that is written while blaze runs and read after a crash also gets a DST (`dst-not-review`) that
crashes it at every point and checks the restore.

## dst-not-review (rule 43)

Code that is concurrent (atomics, locks, lock-free rings, two threads or processes sharing state),
durable (anything written to disk that must survive), crash-recovering, billing or data-deleting is
proven by a deterministic simulation test (DST): one Hegel test that draws an operation sequence,
the fault classes to turn on, crash points and schedules, runs the code as a sans-IO core in the
simulation (`blaze_core::sim::Sim` today, `hegel::sim` as it lands), and checks an oracle that
states the invariant ("every row recorded appears exactly once after any crash"), with planted-bug
controls the oracle must catch and a failing seed that replays. A code review is not evidence that
such code is right: it finds candidates, and each one it finds becomes a case the DST must catch
before the fix lands. A change to such code without a DST that covers it is unfinished, whoever
reviewed it.
